{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-nc-c","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"407af38f5fe5ca33d82090eba91098bbf8aac0934784959093fd0579a8315d11","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nc-class-c:lineage:37","source_registry_sha256":"e128656a3d00ba5437556728ebd87f5842c83601163739613417fe77cf9f423b","source_liveness_sha256":"dbfdf3e6d892a41c42c05809a9213d44a78aedd480dc6de23937c97292428b74"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Passing, backing, parking, intersections and roundabouts","heading":"C — Passing, being passed, parking limits, backing, intersection right of way, traffic circles and roundabouts (North Carolina)","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Passing, being passed, parking limits, backing, intersection right of way, traffic circles and roundabouts (North Carolina)
Knowledge domain: when and how to pass and how to let others pass, where parking is forbidden, how to back safely, who goes first at an intersection, and how to drive through traffic circles and modern roundabouts.

FACT_ID: sec09-F01 | anchor: A01
To pass, first look ahead and behind to judge whether it is safe, then signal to the drivers around you, then sound the horn to alert the driver ahead. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec09-F02 | anchor: A01
Your horn signal puts the driver you are passing under a legal duty to help you get by. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec09-F03 | anchor: A01
Pass only with plenty of room and a steady speed, and only if you can see far enough to get back into your lane before meeting oncoming traffic. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec09-F04 | anchor: A01
The law requires the passing driver to stay at least two feet to the left of the vehicle being passed. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec09-F05 | anchor: A01
Railroad crossings, town and city intersections, and marked intersections in the countryside are places where passing is never safe and is usually against the law. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec09-F06 | anchor: A01
Do not pass on a curve or hill where you cannot see at least 500 feet ahead. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec09-F07 | anchor: A01
Do not pass where a solid yellow line is in your lane or where there is a double solid yellow line. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec09-F08 | anchor: A01
Passing on the right is illegal except where specifically allowed, because it puts you on the other driver's blind side, where that car might turn right or pull over. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec09-F09 | anchor: A01
Passing on the right is allowed on highways with two or more lanes each way, on one-way streets, around a car in a left-turn lane, and when you are in a lane reserved for right turns. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec09-F10 | anchor: A01
On a three-lane highway you may pass only in the center lane where it is marked for passing your way, unless the car in the center lane is turning left. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec09-F11 | anchor: A01
When someone is passing you, you must help: move toward the right edge if they sound the horn, and never speed up. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec09-F12 | anchor: A01
Speeding up and failing to give way to a passing vehicle is a misdemeanor if it leads to a crash with injury or property damage. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec09-F13 | anchor: A02
Park on the right-hand side of the street at all times, unless it is a one-way street. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec09-F14 | anchor: A02
When pulling out of a parallel space, look for approaching traffic and signal a left turn first; the signal is not needed when parked on the left of a one-way street. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec09-F15 | anchor: A02
Do not park at an intersection, in front of a driveway, or on a crosswalk, sidewalk or bridge. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec09-F16 | anchor: A02
Do not park within 25 feet of the curb line of a cross street, or within 15 feet of the intersecting right of way lines where there is no curb. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec09-F17 | anchor: A02
Do not park within 15 feet of a fire hydrant or of a fire station entrance. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec09-F18 | anchor: A02
Never park on the paved travel part of a highway, and parking on the shoulder is illegal unless drivers from both directions can see your vehicle for at least 200 feet. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec09-F19 | anchor: A02
Keep at least one block away from a fire or fire truck inside city limits, and at least 400 feet away outside a city, when parking. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec09-F20 | anchor: A02
Parking is not allowed anywhere in an interstate right of way, except in designated areas or in an emergency. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec09-F21 | anchor: A02
Disabled parking spaces may be used only by a vehicle showing a disability license plate or placard. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec09-F22 | anchor: A02
Before getting in to back up, check behind the vehicle for children or small objects, which are hard to see from the driver's seat. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec09-F23 | anchor: A02
When backing, steer with your left hand and look over your right shoulder through the rear window instead of relying only on the mirrors or side window. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec09-F24 | anchor: A02
Back up very slowly, at no more than 10 mph, because a vehicle is harder to control and stop in reverse. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec09-F25 | anchor: A03
Intersections are where crashes happen most often, and over one-third of fatal motor vehicle crashes occur there. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec09-F26 | anchor: A03
On a four-lane highway divided by a median wider than 30 feet, each crossing counts as a separate intersection. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec09-F27 | anchor: A03
The law requires you to slow down as you approach an intersection, even when you have the right of way. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec09-F28 | anchor: A03
At an intersection with no signs or signals, a vehicle already inside the intersection goes before one that has not entered. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec09-F29 | anchor: A03
When vehicles reach an uncontrolled intersection at the same moment, the vehicle on the right has the right of way. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec09-F30 | anchor: A03
When two facing vehicles arrive together and one wants to turn left, the turning driver must signal and wait, so the driver going straight has the right of way. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec09-F31 | anchor: A03
Never change lanes while driving straight through an intersection. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec09-F32 | anchor: A03
At a stop sign you must stop completely and yield to traffic on the through street before moving on or turning. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec09-F33 | anchor: A03
When coming out of a private driveway, stop and yield to every vehicle and pedestrian, and at a blind unmarked intersection stop and then creep forward carefully. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec09-F34 | anchor: A03
A single-point interchange merges two intersections into one above or below a free-flowing road, run by a single set of traffic signals. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec09-F35 | anchor: A04
A modern roundabout is much smaller than an older traffic circle and keeps speeds low, about 15 to 20 mph, which makes it safer. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec09-F36 | anchor: A04
In a traffic circle all vehicles travel counterclockwise to the right and leave by turning right; with more than one lane, get into the outside lane before your exit and never turn right from an inside lane. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec09-F37 | anchor: A04
A whole traffic circle counts as one intersection, and vehicles already in the circle have the right of way. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec09-F38 | anchor: A05
A yellow roundabout-ahead sign tells you to slow down, and on entry you yield to any vehicles or bicyclists already circulating. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec09-F39 | anchor: A05
Vehicles inside a roundabout do not yield to those approaching; signal when you exit and yield to pedestrians in the roundabout crosswalk. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec09-F40 | anchor: A05
In a single-lane roundabout you go a quarter of the way around to turn right, halfway to go straight, three-quarters to turn left, and all the way around for a U-turn. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec09-F41 | anchor: A05
In a multi-lane roundabout, choose your lane from signs and markings before entering: usually the right lane to exit right and the left lane to go straight, turn left or make a U-turn, with no lane changes inside. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec09-F42 | anchor: A05
Never enter a roundabout while an emergency vehicle with lights and siren is going through; if you are already inside, exit first and then pull over. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec09-F43 | anchor: A05
Drivers should not pass a bicyclist inside a roundabout, and pedestrians should use the marked crosswalks around the outside rather than cutting through the middle. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0061]

Misconceptions: a driver being passed must not speed up and must help the passer; passing on the right is not generally allowed just because there is room; having the right of way does not excuse you from slowing at an intersection; cars in a roundabout do not yield to entering cars; in a multi-lane roundabout you pick your lane before entering, not inside it.
Mnemonics: look, signal, horn, then pass; the car on the right goes first when arrivals tie; a left turn waits for straight traffic; quarter right, half straight, three-quarters left, full circle back.
Glossary: double parking means parking on the roadway side of another parked vehicle; interchange means roads crossing at different levels with ramps; single-point interchange means one signal-controlled intersection over or under a through road; roundabout means a small circular intersection with counterclockwise flow; truck apron means the raised concrete island trucks may use in a roundabout.
Dynamic facts: posted no-parking signs add restrictions wherever they appear; the distances here are the fixed rules the handbook prints.
